newsitem.title: USA: Blue Shield of California in $12 million settlement.
newsitem.headline: Blue Shield of California in $12 million settlement.

text.p: Blue Shield of California has agreed to pay $12 million to the U.S. government to settle allegations that it submitted false claims for payment under a contract to process Medicare claims, officials said Friday.
The U.S. Department of Justice and the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services announced they had reached the agreement with the company.

The agreement settles a civil lawsuit alleging that Blue Shield of California, based in San Francisco, covered up claims processing errors from Health Care Financing Administration auditors to obtain more favourable scores under a programme for grading the carrier's claims processing capabilities.

"Maintaining the integrity of the claims handling processes by Medicare contractors, who are on the front lines of defending against Medicare fraud, is an important enforcement goal," Michael Yamaguchi, U.S. Attorney for northern California, said in a statement.

The agreement settles a so-called "whistleblower" lawsuit filed on behalf of the United States by Weldon Dodson, who used to work for Blue Shield's Medicare Division in Chico, California, the U.S. Attorney's office said.
Until September 1996, Blue Shield was the Medicare carrier for the Health Care Financing Administration in northern and central California, it said.

The company was reimbursed more than $40 million a year by the federal government to process about 20 million claims submitted for doctors' services, laboratory services and other claims covered under Part B of the federal Medicare programme.

Dodson alleged that some employees in Blue Shield's Medicare division in Chico and Marysville, California, altered or discarded documents that would have disclosed claims processing errors, substituted backdated and altered documents for documents that contained errors, and rigged purportedly random samples of files to deceive Health Care Financing Administration auditors into believing that Blue Shield's performance was better than it actually was.

Lisa Citron, a spokeswoman for Blue Shield of California, said a small number of employees was responsible for the violations and that the company did not know about them. Thirteen employees were dismissed in 1994 as a result, she said.

Citron said Blue Shield had "accepted responsibility for the misconduct of a small number of employees who violated Blue Shield policies and government audit procedures. We took prompt corrective measures."
